lessons.title: Principles of Annealing: Stress Relief
lessons.body: When glass cools unevenly, internal stresses build up that can cause it to crack or shatter unexpectedly. Annealing is the controlled cooling process that relieves these stresses. In a small workshop in Nairobi or Lagos, you might make glass beads, fused glass art, or even simple window panes. After shaping the hot glass, you must cool it slowly through a specific temperature range. For soda-lime glass, the annealing point is around 540Â°C. At this temperature, the glass is still slightly plastic and can relieve stress in about 15 minutes. Then you cool it slowly to the strain point, about 510Â°C, where stress is frozen in if cooled too fast. The key is to keep the glass at the annealing point long enough for all parts to reach the same temperature, then cool at a controlled rate, usually 1-2Â°C per minute for thick pieces. A simple annealing oven, called a lehr, can be made from firebricks and a PID controller. Without annealing, glass may look fine but break from a slight bump or temperature change. In Africa, where daily temperature swings can be large, proper annealing is critical for durable products. Always test your annealed glass by checking for stress with a polariscope, which shows stress patterns as colored bands. If you see bright colors, you need to adjust your cooling schedule. Remember, annealing is not just about cooling; it's about giving the glass time to relax internally.

lessons.title: Annealing Lehr Design and Operation
lessons.body: A lehr is a specialized oven for annealing glass. For small-scale operations in Africa, you can build a simple lehr using locally available materials. The body can be made from a 200-litre steel drum lined with ceramic fiber insulation. Heating elements from old electric stoves or kanthal wire can be used, controlled by a PID temperature controller with a thermocouple. The lehr should have a ramp-up zone, a soaking zone, and a slow cooling zone. For a batch lehr, you load glass, heat to 540Â°C, hold for 30 minutes, then cool at 1Â°C per minute to 400Â°C, then faster to room temperature. For continuous lehrs, like those used in larger workshops, glass moves on a conveyor through zones. In Africa, many artisans use a programmable kiln for annealing. The key is even temperature distribution. Use a fan to circulate air if possible. Place thermocouples at different points to monitor. A common mistake is opening the lehr door too early, causing thermal shock. Wait until the glass is below 100Â°C. You can test the lehr by annealing a test piece and checking stress with a polariscope. If stress is high, adjust the cooling rate. Also, ensure the lehr is level and free from drafts. In hot climates, the lehr may need extra insulation to maintain temperature stability. Regular maintenance includes checking thermocouples and heating elements. With a well-designed lehr, you can produce consistently strong glass products.

lessons.title: Tempering: Thermal and Chemical
lessons.body: Tempering makes glass stronger by creating compressive stress on its surface. Thermal tempering involves heating glass to about 620-680Â°C, then rapidly cooling it with air jets. This causes the surface to cool faster than the interior, putting the surface into compression and the interior into tension. The result is glass that is 4-5 times stronger than annealed glass. In Africa, thermal tempering is used for car windows, shower doors, and building facades. However, it requires precise control. You need a tempering furnace with rollers and air blowers. The glass must be cut and edged before tempering because any cutting after will cause it to shatter. Chemical tempering, also called ion exchange, is done by immersing glass in a molten salt bath, usually potassium nitrate, at about 400-450Â°C. Smaller sodium ions in the glass are replaced by larger potassium ions, creating surface compression. This method is used for thin glass, like smartphone screens. In Africa, chemical tempering is less common due to the cost of salts and equipment, but it can be done in small tanks. Safety is critical: molten salt can cause severe burns. Always wear protective gear. Both methods require strict quality control. Tempered glass breaks into small, blunt pieces, which is a safety feature. You can test tempered glass by hitting it with a hammer; it should shatter into tiny fragments. If it breaks into large shards, it's not properly tempered.

lessons.title: Tempering Furnace Operation
lessons.body: Operating a tempering furnace requires attention to detail. First, preheat the furnace to the required temperature, typically 650Â°C for 6mm glass. Load the glass on ceramic rollers, ensuring it is clean and free of dust. Any dirt will cause defects. The glass moves through the furnace on rollers, heated by electric elements or gas burners. The heating time depends on thickness: for 6mm glass, about 2-3 minutes per mm, so 12-18 minutes. The glass must reach a uniform temperature. Then it quickly moves to the quenching section, where air jets at 0.5-1.5 bar cool it rapidly. The air pressure and nozzle design determine the cooling rate. After quenching, the glass is checked for flatness and stress. A polariscope can reveal stress patterns. In Africa, many small tempering setups use modified pizza ovens or custom-built furnaces. It's crucial to have a backup power source, as power cuts can ruin the glass and damage the furnace. Also, maintain the rollers; they must be smooth and parallel to avoid marking the glass. Regular calibration of thermocouples is essential. If the furnace overheats, glass may warp or break. If underheated, tempering will be incomplete. Always follow the manufacturer's guidelines. For safety, wear heat-resistant gloves and face shield. After tempering, allow the glass to cool to room temperature before handling. Test a sample from each batch by breaking it; it should fragment into small pieces. If not, adjust the furnace settings. Record all parameters for consistency.

lessons.title: Fragmentation Testing and Standards
lessons.body: Fragmentation testing is how you verify that glass is properly tempered. The standard test involves breaking a sample and counting the number of fragments in a 50mm x 50mm square. According to ISO 12543 and EN 12150, tempered glass must break into at least 40 fragments in that area for 4mm glass, and more for thicker glass. The fragments should be small, blunt, and relatively uniform. To perform the test, take a tempered glass sample, place it flat on a surface, and strike it with a sharp tool at a point about 20mm from the edge. The glass should shatter into tiny pieces. Collect the fragments and count them in the central area. If the count is low or if there are large shards, the tempering is inadequate. In Africa, many workshops use this simple test to ensure quality. You can also use a polariscope to see stress patterns; properly tempered glass shows a uniform stress pattern. For chemical tempered glass, the test is similar, but the fragment count may differ. Standards also require that tempered glass not have any bubbles, scratches, or edge defects that could cause spontaneous breakage. Spontaneous breakage can occur due to nickel sulfide inclusions, which expand over time. To reduce this risk, use high-quality glass and proper tempering. Always document your test results. If your glass fails, review your furnace operation, cooling rate, and glass quality. Consistency is key to meeting standards and satisfying customers.

lessons.title: Quality Control of Annealed and Tempered Glass
lessons.body: Quality control (QC) ensures that every piece of glass meets the required standards. For annealed glass, QC focuses on stress levels and optical distortion. Use a polariscope to check for stress; a properly annealed piece shows minimal color bands. Also, inspect for bubbles, stones, and scratches. For tempered glass, QC includes checking flatness, fragmentation, and surface compression. Measure surface compression with a surface stress meter, which should read at least 69 MPa (10,000 psi) for thermally tempered glass. In Africa, you can use a simple polariscope and a fragmentation test as primary QC tools. Establish a sampling plan: test at least one piece per batch. Keep records of furnace temperature, cooling rate, and test results. Calibrate your equipment regularly. Train workers to identify defects. Common defects in tempered glass include warp, roller marks, and edge damage. Warp can be caused by uneven heating or cooling; adjust the furnace. Roller marks come from dirty rollers; clean them. Edge damage from poor handling; train workers to handle with care. For annealed glass, slow cooling is critical; if you see stress, re-anneal. Also, consider the end use: glass for a tabletop may need different QC than glass for a building. Always follow customer specifications and national standards. In Africa, organizations like the Kenya Bureau of Standards provide guidelines. By implementing strict QC, you reduce waste, increase customer trust, and build a reputation for quality.
